about.title: About the rural exodus
about.subtitle: Exodus — an artistic experience by Jacinto Costoso

sections.title: Walking, looking, remembering
paragraphs: With Exodus I am developing an artistic experience around walking, landscape and displacement, in memory of Spain’s rural exodus.

Huertahernando remains the starting village and the project’s point of reference. From this territory you can reach the globe, search for a place and select an area to explore. The program builds its terrain, and an autonomous walker searches for a route between the points you place, taking the slopes into account.

sections.title: Comparing landscapes
paragraphs: Open the “1956–57 colorized” layer and compare it with the recent “Spring” and “Winter” images. Look at the small plots, paths, cultivated land and places reclaimed by vegetation. Press C to switch between maps.
The 1956–57 colours are reconstructed; the landscape details come from the historical photograph. Its original black-and-white version is still available in edit mode.

sections.title: A history of departures
paragraphs: The rural exodus was a profound rupture, experienced in the continuing hardship of the post-war years. After the Spanish Civil War of 1936–1939, Franco’s regime imposed autarky. From 1939 to 1952, ration cards accompanied years of hunger, shortages and poverty.
From the 1950s onwards, millions of Spaniards left the countryside, some for cities and others for countries abroad. The great rural exodus of 1950–1975 was particularly intense in the 1960s.

These departures cannot be reduced to an inevitable consequence of modernisation. They also belong to the history of a rural Spain impoverished and weakened by Francoist policies. Exodus takes a critical view of that history through landscapes, gestures and the memory of those who had to leave.

fiction.title: Tea from the Tagus
fiction.subtitle: A Castilian tale
paragraphs: In Huertahernando, people said the Tagus belonged to everyone, but its banks belonged to those who knew where to put their feet.
It was a manner of speaking. In the villages of the Upper Tagus, people had always liked sweeping statements, especially when they had little to say.

The river ran along the bottom of its gorges, between junipers, box trees and honey-coloured rock faces. In summer the stones grew so hot you could fry an egg on them. In winter the wind came down from the mountains with a particular viciousness, as though it had some old score to settle with the inhabitants.

In that country lived Eusebio, seventy-eight years old, a former shepherd, owner of three goats, a mule that had been dead for fifteen years, and a house whose roof was threatening to join it in the graveyard.
Eusebio had one peculiarity: he never drank coffee.
— Coffee, he would say, is for people in a hurry. I have never been in a hurry for anything, not even to die.
Every morning he heated water in an old enamel saucepan and added a few leaves of wild mint that he gathered on the banks of the Tagus.
He called it river tea.
His father had drunk it, and his grandfather before him, and probably a few ancestors whom nobody remembered any more. The recipe was simple: water, a few leaves and the patience to wait.
One October morning, his neighbour Julián walked into his house without knocking.

Julián had been the town clerk for thirty-two years. Since retiring, he still behaved as though the municipal registers belonged to him. He knew every neighbour’s name, their parents’ names, their creditors’ names and, sometimes, even the names of their real fathers.
— Eusebio, do you know you are a criminal?
The old man looked up from the saucepan.
— Since when?
— Since you started picking your tea.
— Is that so? What was I before?
— Before, you were simply an idiot.
— Well, I have made progress.
Julián did not smile. He pulled a printed sheet covered in tiny lettering from his pocket.
— Apparently some parts of the park are protected. You cannot just gather whatever you like.
— And where are these parts?
— That is precisely the problem.
— Have they disappeared?
— No. They are on a map.
— Then show me the map.
— I do not have it.
— Have you lost it?
— I have never found it.
Eusebio poured the infusion into two chipped cups.
— A fine invention, he said. A map nobody can find that forbids you to go to certain places.
Julián took his cup.
— Apparently they can fine you.
— How much?
— Perhaps five hundred euros.
Eusebio slowly set the saucepan on the table.
— Five hundred euros?
— So they say.
— For how many leaves?
— That I do not know.
The old man thought for a moment.
— If I pick five leaves, that is a hundred euros each. More expensive than saffron.
They drank in silence.
Then Eusebio asked:
— What if I pick just one leaf?
— I suppose it depends on the officer.
— Then it is not a law. It is a mood.
A few days later, a man from Madrid arrived in the village.

His name was Tomás Valverde. He was fifty-nine, with round glasses and an old Peugeot whose doors did not close properly. He had come to spend a few weeks in his mother’s house. She had died that spring.

Tomás had grown up in Madrid, but he had spent every summer of his childhood in the valley. He knew the paths, the springs, the ruined sheep shelters and the pools where wild boar wallowed. Yet he had committed an unforgivable mistake: he had lived elsewhere.
That was why, in the bar, they called him the Madrileño.
He had been coming to the village for forty years. They would probably go on calling him that until the day he died.
One afternoon, Tomás went down towards the Tagüenza Bridge with Eusebio. The old man wanted to show him a place where especially fragrant mint grew.
The path wound between the rocks. Vultures circled above the cliffs. From time to time they heard a stone falling into the ravine, followed by an immense silence.
When they reached the water, Eusebio knelt down with difficulty.
— Look. This is it.
Tomás rubbed a leaf between his fingers.
— It smells wonderful.
— Naturally. It grows here.
— And in other places?
— In other places it smells of other places.
Eusebio cut a few stems with his old pocketknife.
Tomás watched him.
— Are you sure we are allowed to pick it?
The old man sighed.
— Are you going to start as well?
— Julián told me about the regulations.
— Julián spent thirty years making paperwork. Now he thinks the world is made of paper.
They were climbing back towards the path when a green vehicle appeared behind the pines.
Two officers got out.
The first was a sturdy man of about fifty, with a grey moustache. The second, much younger, carried a notebook and looked around with the attention of someone still trying to understand his job.
— Good afternoon.
— Afternoon, replied Eusebio.
The older officer immediately recognised the shepherd.
— Eusebio! Are you still alive?
— Much to my regret, answered the old man. And are you still a civil servant?
They burst out laughing.
The officer noticed the little bunch of mint.
— What have you got there?
— Marijuana. But do not tell the priest.
Another burst of laughter.
Then the officer looked at Tomás.
— And you, sir?
— I am from Madrid. Well, my family is from here.
— Ah.
There was something final about that simple “ah”.
The young officer asked to see what Tomás had in his bag. He found a few mint leaves gathered a few minutes earlier.
— Are you aware that gathering plants may be regulated within the park?
Tomás answered calmly:
— That is precisely what we are trying to find out: where it is permitted.
— It depends on the zones.
— Which ones?
The young man hesitated.
— We would have to consult the maps.
— Do you have them?
— Not with me, no.
— And where can they be consulted?
— At the appropriate department.
— Do you know the address?
The young officer looked at his colleague.
The older man was beginning to find the conversation rather tiresome.
— Look, sir. We are not going to spend the whole afternoon arguing over four leaves.
— I entirely agree. I am only asking where the boundary is.
— The boundaries are established in the regulations.
— I do not doubt it. But where do they run?
The older officer’s tone grew sharper.
— Are you questioning my authority?
Tomás was taken aback.
— Not at all. I am asking you a question.
— Then I suggest you do not make things difficult.
Eusebio, who had listened without speaking, intervened:
— He is not making anything difficult. He wants to know where he can pick his tea.
The officer placed a hand on his shoulder.
— You go home, Eusebio. And look after those knees.
Then he turned towards Tomás.
— And you, sir, let me see your identity papers.
By the next day, the whole village knew about the incident.
In the bar on the square, the versions multiplied.
According to the baker, Tomás had insulted the officers.
According to the baker’s wife, he had threatened to report them.
According to the mayor’s cousin, he had announced his intention to report the entire regional administration to Brussels.
In fact, Tomás had merely asked for a map.
But under certain circumstances, a map can become an extremely dangerous object.
Julián advised him to let it go.
— They have not fined you. Why look for trouble?
— Because I want to understand.
— That is precisely what I object to.
— Wanting to understand?
— Wanting to understand what nobody has asked you to understand.
Tomás laughed out loud.
— You were the town clerk for thirty years, Julián. Surely you know where to find a regulation.
— Of course.
— Then help me.
Julián looked towards the door of the bar and lowered his voice.
— I could. But I would rather not get involved.
— Why?
— Because my nephew works at the Provincial Delegation. And his wife is waiting for a transfer.
Tomás fell silent.
He had just understood something no map could have taught him.
Two weeks passed.

Tomás wrote to the regional administration. He politely requested a detailed map of the strictly protected zones around Huertahernando and the Tagüenza Bridge, together with the provisions governing the gathering of aromatic plants for personal use.
First he received an automated acknowledgement.
Then a second message informed him that his request had been forwarded to the appropriate department.
Finally, a third told him that this department had requested a report from another department.
Tomás printed the three letters.
He showed them to Eusebio.
— See? They are dealing with it.
The old man examined the papers.
— Three letters for a mint leaf. At this rate, they will run out of paper.
A month later, a reply arrived.
It quoted several articles, two decrees, a management plan and a regional order. It explained that gathering activities were subject to the applicable provisions according to environmental zoning.
No map was enclosed.
Tomás read the document several times.
Then he went to the town hall.
The mayor, Don Anselmo, was a genial man who had learned never to say no when he could say “we will look into the matter”.
He received Tomás in his office, beneath a portrait of the king.
— My dear Tomás! How is your mother’s house?
— Still standing.
— That is what matters.
Tomás explained his problem.
The mayor listened with increasing benevolence, which gradually turned into concern.
— But why do you insist on having that map?
— So I know where gathering plants is prohibited.
— And why do you want to know?
— To obey the law.
Don Anselmo interlaced his fingers.
— You must understand, Tomás, that we have always lived in harmony with the park here.
— I think that is wonderful.
— We avoid unnecessary conflicts.
— So do I.
— Then why do you want to create one?
Tomás contemplated the portrait of the king.
— I am not creating any conflict. I am asking where a boundary runs.
The mayor stood up, signalling that the interview was over.
— Take my advice. Go walking, enjoy the river, take photographs. But leave the regulations alone.
— And the mint?
Don Anselmo smiled.
— Have you never heard of the little bags they sell in the supermarket?
Winter came.

The first frosts whitened the roofs of Huertahernando. The villagers stored their firewood, repaired their chimneys and prepared for those long evenings when the village seemed abandoned by the rest of the world.
One morning, Eusebio did not appear at the bar.
It was unlike him.
Julián went to his house and found him sitting beside the stove, wrapped in a blanket.
He had a fever.
Tomás took him to the medical centre. It was nothing too serious, the doctor said, but at his age he had to take care of himself.
For a few days, Tomás called on him every morning.
Eusebio had lost his appetite. He wanted neither coffee, nor milk, nor broth.
— I want my tea, he said one evening.
Tomás looked at the box where the old man usually kept his dried leaves.
It was empty.
— I will buy you some.
— I do not want your shop tea.
— But it is mint too.
— Then buy me a bottled river as well, while you are at it.
Tomás smiled.
The next day, he went down to the Tagus.
The winter sun lit the rock faces. The water flowed cold and clear between the moss-covered stones.
He found the place Eusebio had shown him.
A few mint stems still remained, sheltered in a small damp hollow.
He knelt down.
He took out his knife.
And then he stopped.
He thought of the officer, the town hall, the letters, the regulations, the possibility of a penalty whose exact conditions he still did not know.
Above all, he thought of the mayor’s words: Leave the regulations alone.
He put his knife away.
For a long time he stood motionless before the plants.
Then he climbed back to the village with empty hands.
Eusebio died in February.
They buried him on a Saturday, beneath a perfectly blue sky.
There were few people in the cemetery: the villagers, some relatives from Guadalajara, the mayor, Julián and the two park officers, who had known the old shepherd since they were children.
After the burial, the men gathered in the bar.
They spoke of Eusebio, his goats, his jokes and his extraordinary ability to get through winters in shoes full of holes.
Then Julián told the story of the tea.
They all burst out laughing.
Even the officer with the grey moustache, who had come to offer his condolences.
— That Eusebio! he said. All the mint he must have drunk in his lifetime!
Tomás, sitting at the end of the table, looked up.
— By the way, he asked, was he allowed to pick it?
Silence fell.
The officer set his glass on the table.
— That story again?
— I am only asking a question.
— You are not going to start again.
— No. I would just like an answer.
The mayor intervened:
— Tomás, we are burying a friend today.
— Precisely.
Nobody understood what he meant.
Or perhaps they all understood far too well.
Julián kicked him under the table.
Tomás fell silent.
The following spring, a small envelope arrived from Guadalajara.
It contained another administrative reply.

It explained that the requested cartographic documents could be consulted in accordance with the procedures established by the appropriate departments, and that certain geographical information could be obtained from the managing authority.
There was still no map.
Tomás placed the letter on the table.
He now had a twenty-seven-page file for a question that, in Spanish, took just eleven words:
Where is it permitted to gather a few mint leaves beside the Tagus?
He looked at the papers for a long time.
Then he opened the window.
In the distance the mountains were green. Swallows had returned to the rooftops. The river still ran through the bottom of the valley, indifferent to the regulations of men.
Tomás picked up Eusebio’s old tin box, which Julián had given him after the funeral.
Inside it, a single dry leaf remained, forgotten in a corner.
He gently took it between his fingers.
It hardly had any scent left.
Then at last he understood what had escaped him all those months.
Nobody had formally forbidden him to gather that mint. Nobody had shown him where he could do it. Nobody had convicted him.
And yet he had stopped picking it.
It had required no trial, no judge, not even a fine.
An uncertainty, a few looks, some friendly advice and that ancient fear of displeasing those with a little power had been enough.
He closed the box.
The following Sunday, he went down to the Tagus.
He walked a long way before finding the little clumps of mint growing between the stones.
This time he did not take out his knife.
He simply sat on a rock and watched the water pass.
A boy of about ten appeared on the path, accompanied by his grandfather.
The child saw the mint.
— Grandad, what is that plant?
— River tea, son.
— Can we pick it?
The grandfather looked at Tomás.
Tomás looked at the grandfather.
The two men hesitated.
At last the old man answered:
— Once, yes.
— And now?
The grandfather lowered his eyes towards the river.
— Now I do not know.
The child thought for a few seconds.
— And who does know?
Nobody answered.
Above them, a vulture slowly traced its circles in the Castilian sky.
The Tagus continued on its course, as it had long before kingdoms, borders, town halls and nature parks.
And on its bank, three generations of men contemplated a small plant that asked for nothing but to grow.

The youngest had just learned his first lesson in citizenship: in his country he could inherit the land, the language and the memories of his ancestors, but not necessarily the freedom of their gestures.
That day nobody gathered mint.
And nobody could say whether it was out of respect for nature, respect for the law or, quite simply, fear.
